label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: A prolonged arctic outbreak lasts 15 days. Load peaks 12% above a normal winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.12), and Henry Hub rises 40% (gas_hh_pct 40). Gas pipelines into downstate are constrained, so N.Y.C. prices decouple from WEST, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 150). The retail load obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and scales with load, so it loses about $4,650 per $/MWh-day of widening. P2 recovers only about $770 of that. The WEST-long positions P1 and P4 gain a little from higher load and gas, roughly $1M over the period, which offsets only a small part of the spread loss. A $5/MWh gas basis premium (ny_gas_basis_usd 5) trims P4 further. No spikes, no ref_onpeak or dart shocks are applied, so the loss is purely congestion and zone volume. Net loss is about $7.5M by linear scaling of the winter sensitivities, which are one-at-a-time and not additive, so this is an approximation.

A Winter Storm Elliott-style flash freeze lasts 7 days, with forced outages and import curtailments concentrated downstate. The real-time N.Y.C. minus WEST spread blows out by $300/MWh on top of the base spread (pocket_minus_ref_usd 300), comparable to the analogue's 338.5 $/MWh. Real-time clears 120% above day-ahead (dart_pct 120), as in Elliott, which hurts the day-ahead-minus-real-time receiver P3. Load is only slightly above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03), because Elliott had curtailments rather than record demand. Gas rises 20% (gas_hh_pct 20), with a $8 N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 8) that cuts the P4 payoff. The N.Y.C. short in P5 loses roughly $4,650 per $/MWh-day, so about $9.8M over 7 days. P2 offsets about $1.6M. Gains on P1 and P4 from the dart and gas moves are about $0.7M. Net loss is about $7M. Estimate is by linear scaling of one-at-a-time sensitivities.

A 20-day cold spell traps gas and power downstate. Load is 8% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.08) and Henry Hub is up 15% (gas_hh_pct 15). N.Y.C. is import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100). Upstate has surplus wind and hydro, so WEST on-peak falls 30% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -30). This removes the P1 and P4 gains, because the long WEST swap and heat-rate call lose value, and it adds to P5 losses through the load scaling. The hedge in P5 is long WEST, so lower WEST prices also hurt that leg. Spread losses are about $7.8M (P5 net of P2), and the WEST decline and gas rise roughly cancel the load gains on P1 and P4. No spikes and no dart shock are applied, so the loss comes from congestion plus the system and gas channels. Stated loss is a conservative $7M, from linear scaling of non-additive sensitivities.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long cold winter lasts 30 days with a persistent but moderate downstate squeeze. Load runs 6% above a normal winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.06) and Henry Hub is 10% higher (gas_hh_pct 10), a mild cold-snap gas response. Downstate gas and transmission constraints keep the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread $60/MWh wider than normal (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60) for the whole month. A $2/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) trims the P4 payoff. The loss comes from the retail obligation P5, which is short N.Y.C. and scales with load. It loses roughly $4,400 per $/MWh-day of widening, about $7.9M over the month. P2 offsets about $1.4M. The long WEST positions P1 and P4 gain roughly $0.7M from load and gas, and higher load adds about $0.4M to the P5 loss. There are no spikes or dart shocks. The net is roughly -$6.2M, from linear scaling of one-at-a-time sensitivities that are not additive, so this is an approximation.

A 25-day cold spell tightens downstate supply while upstate stays comparatively soft. Load is 8% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.08) and Henry Hub is 8% higher (gas_hh_pct 8). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $70/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70) because import limits and gas constraints bind into the city. WEST on-peak is 20% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -20), reflecting upstate surplus and mild local conditions. This erodes the gains on the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4, and it hurts the long-WEST hedge leg inside P5. The spread widening costs P5 about $7.7M over 25 days, and P2 offsets about $1.35M. The WEST decline and higher load mean P1 and P4 contribute only small gains or losses. There are no spikes, dart or basis shocks. The net is about -$6.3M. This is a linear approximation from non-additive one-at-a-time sensitivities.

A sharp 12-day cold episode hits the city hard through a gas-delivery squeeze. Load is only 3% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03), and Henry Hub is up just 5% (gas_hh_pct 5), so the pain is local rather than system-wide. N.Y.C. gas is tight, so a $4/MMBtu basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 4) lowers the P4 payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $120/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), which hurts the retail short P5 by about $6.5M over 12 days. P2 offsets about $1.1M. WEST on-peak is 15% below the gas and load implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -15) as upstate generation is plentiful. That cuts the gains on P1 and P4 and lowers the value of the P5 WEST hedge. There are no spikes or dart shocks, so the loss is congestion and zone volume plus small system and gas effects. The net is about -$5.5M, by linear scaling of non-additive sensitivities, so treat it as approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 10-day deep freeze hits the city. Load runs 4% above a normal winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.04), kept below the level the engine flagged as implausible. Henry Hub is up 20% (gas_hh_pct 20) and the N.Y.C. gas basis is $6/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 6), which trims the P4 heat-rate payoff. Import and gas constraints widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $200/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 200). Real-time clears 100% above day-ahead (dart_pct 100), which hurts the P3 receiver. The retail short P5 loses about $4,400 per $/MWh-day of widening, roughly $8.8M over 10 days. P2 offsets about $1.2M, and P1 and P4 gain about $1.2M from the real-time and gas moves. The net is about -$6M, from linear scaling of one-at-a-time sensitivities that are not additive.

A 20-day cold spell stresses the city while upstate stays well supplied. Load is 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05) and Henry Hub is 5% higher (gas_hh_pct 5), a mild gas response. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $80/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80) because downstate import limits bind. WEST on-peak falls 35% below the level gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -35) on surplus upstate generation. That shrinks the P1 swap and P4 call gains and weakens the long-WEST hedge inside P5. The spread widening costs P5 about $6.6M over 20 days. P2 offsets about $1.0M, and the WEST decline costs P1 and P4 about $0.4M net of the load and gas gains. There are no spikes, dart or basis shocks. The net is about -$6M, from a linear approximation of non-additive sensitivities.

A violent 8-day burst of cold sends city prices far above upstate while system demand rises only slightly. Load is 2% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.02) and Henry Hub is 10% higher (gas_hh_pct 10). The N.Y.C. gas basis is $3/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 3), which cuts the P4 payoff a little. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 250), inside the historical maximum for winter. WEST on-peak is 10% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -10), so P1 and P4 gain almost nothing. P5 loses about $4,100 per $/MWh-day, roughly $8.2M over 8 days. P2 offsets about $1.3M, and the other positions lose about $0.2M. The net is about -$6.5M, from linear scaling of one-at-a-time sensitivities that are not additive.

scenario.narrative: A month-long summer heat pattern lifts the daily peak load to 1.10 times normal. NYC import constraints from upstate bind on most days, so I add 70 $/MWh to the NYC-minus-WEST spread for 30 days. The retail load obligation P5 is short NYC and hedged only with WEST, so it loses on every hour of the widening, and the loss grows with load. P2 gains only a small part of this because it is just 25 MW. Strong upstate supply and imports hold WEST on-peak 30% below what the load shock alone implies, which cuts the gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Gas, DART and spikes are left unshocked, because raising WEST prices or gas would only help the long positions. The estimate scales the one-at-a-time sensitivities (about 3.4k USD per spread dollar-day net of P2) and is uncertain by perhaps 30%.

An intense three-and-a-half-week heat dome pushes peak load to 1.20 times a typical summer day, still inside the historical maximum of 1.514. NYC is isolated by transmission limits and local generation shortfalls, so the NYC-minus-WEST spread widens by 110 $/MWh for 25 days. That is below the historical maximum widening of 289.7. P5, the short NYC retail obligation hedged only by WEST, takes the main loss, and the higher load multiplies its exposure. WEST on-peak is 20% lower than the load and gas effects imply, because upstate has surplus supply while NYC is constrained. That trims the gains on P1 and P4, which would otherwise offset part of the loss. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero, since they would help the long WEST positions. The net estimate is the spread loss on P5 less the P2 gain, partly offset by the load gains on P1 and P4, scaled from the sensitivities. It carries material uncertainty.

A 30-day heat wave raises the peak load modestly to 1.05 times normal. The NYC pocket tightens while upstate WEST prices decouple lower, with WEST on-peak 60% below what the load shock implies. The cause is surplus upstate hydro, wind and import supply that cannot reach NYC. This hits the long WEST swap P1 (100 MW) and the heat-rate call P4 directly. At the same time the NYC-minus-WEST spread widens by 60 $/MWh for 30 days, which hurts the retail load obligation P5 far more than it helps P2. The loss therefore comes from two channels at once, system level and zone volume. Gas, DART and spike shocks stay at zero, since they would raise WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate adds the WEST price decline on P1 and P4 to the spread loss, using scaled one-at-a-time sensitivities. It is uncertain, and the negative WEST move of this size is not itself a heat-wave signature.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer heat pattern leaves load at the normal-day level (ratio 1.0), so no load gain accrues to the long WEST positions. Upstate is oversupplied, with strong hydro, wind and import flows, so WEST on-peak is 75% below what the load and gas shocks imply. This is close to the historical minimum of -89.8%. It directly hurts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. NYC import limits still bind, so I add a moderate 40 $/MWh to the NYC-minus-WEST spread for all 30 days. That hurts the short-NYC retail load P5 by more than it helps P2. The loss comes from the system channel and the zone-volume channel together. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero because they would lift WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate scales the one-at-a-time sensitivities: about -2.2M on P1, -0.8M on P4, -4.3M on P5 and +0.7M on P2. It is uncertain by roughly 30%.

A 30-day heat dome lifts the daily peak load to 1.25 times a typical summer day, well inside the historical maximum of 1.514. The extra load scales up the short NYC retail obligation P5 by about 25%. NYC transmission and local generation constraints widen the NYC-minus-WEST spread by 55 $/MWh on every day. This is the main loss driver, through zone volume on P5, and P2 recovers only a small part of it. WEST on-peak is set 60% below what the load shock implies, because upstate has surplus supply that cannot reach the city. That wipes out the load gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Gas, DART and spikes are zero because they would help the long positions. The estimate is about -7.1M on P5, +1.0M on P2 and roughly -0.3M net on P1 and P4, from scaled sensitivities. It is uncertain, and the engine loss may differ materially.

A 30-day heat wave raises peak load to 1.15 times normal. Constrained NYC import paths widen the NYC-minus-WEST spread by 45 $/MWh for the full 30 days, which is the main loss on the short-NYC retail load P5. WEST on-peak is 70% below the level the load shock implies, as upstate surplus supply holds WEST down. That hurts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A local gas basis of +3 $/MMBtu raises the fuel cost used by P4, which adds 24 $/MWh to the heat-rate strike and reduces the call payoff further. This is the gas channel, and P4 can lose at most its base payoff. Henry Hub, DART and spike shocks are zero because they would raise WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate is about -5.5M on P5, +0.8M on P2, -1.1M on P1 and -0.6M on P4. It is uncertain by perhaps 30%.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A two-week intense heat spell leaves peak load at the typical summer level (ratio 1.0), so the long WEST positions get no load gain. NYC is electrically squeezed by import limits and local unit derates. I add 130 $/MWh to the NYC-minus-WEST spread for 15 days, well below the historical maximum of 289.7. This is the main loss driver. The short-NYC retail obligation P5, hedged only with WEST, loses about 3.4k USD per spread dollar-day, and P2 recovers only its 25 MW share. WEST on-peak is 40% below what the load and gas shocks imply, because upstate has surplus hydro, wind and imports that cannot reach the city. That costs the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 a modest amount. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero because they would lift WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate is roughly -6.7M on P5, +1.2M on P2 and -0.8M net on P1 and P4, scaled from the one-at-a-time sensitivities. It is uncertain by about 30%.

A month-long summer heat pattern lifts peak load 10% above a typical day, while a weak gas market pulls Henry Hub down 35%, inside the historical minimum of -44.2%. Lower fuel cost pushes WEST power down and cuts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Upstate oversupply adds a further 40% decline in WEST on-peak beyond what load and gas imply. NYC import constraints widen the NYC-minus-WEST spread by 50 $/MWh for all 30 days. That hurts the short-NYC retail load P5, and its exposure grows with the 10% extra load. P2 offsets only a small part. This scenario therefore mixes the gas channel, the system channel and zone volume. DART and spike shocks are zero because they would raise WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate is about -5.7M on P5, +0.9M on P2, -2M on P1 net of load gains and -0.7M on P4. Effects are not additive, so it is uncertain.

A 24-day heat pattern raises peak load 8% above a typical summer day, a mild uplift well inside the historical range. NYC local generation shortfalls and import limits widen the NYC-minus-WEST spread by 85 $/MWh for those 24 days. The short-NYC retail obligation P5, hedged only with WEST, takes the main loss, and the load uplift scales its exposure. P2 gains from the same widening, but its 25 MW size recovers only about 15% of the loss. WEST on-peak is 55% below the load-implied level because upstate has surplus supply behind the constraint, which removes the load gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 and turns them into modest losses. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero because they would help the long positions. The duration is 24 days and the shocks apply throughout. The estimate is about -7.5M on P5, +1.2M on P2, +0.7M from load on P1 and P4, and -1.8M from the WEST decline, net near -7M and scaled down for uncertainty.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Henry Hub falls 40%, inside the historical minimum of -44.2%, which lowers fuel cost and the WEST power price. An extra 60% fall in WEST on-peak reflects upstate surplus hydro, wind and imports that cannot reach the city. Together these hit the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. NYC import limits widen the NYC-minus-WEST spread by 40 $/MWh on every day, which hurts the short-NYC retail load P5, hedged only with WEST. P2 recovers only a small part of that loss. DART and spike shocks are zero because they would lift WEST prices and help the long positions. The estimate scales the one-at-a-time sensitivities: about -4.1M on P5, +0.7M on P2, -2.0M on P1 and -0.8M on P4. It is uncertain by roughly 30%.

NYC is squeezed by import limits and local derates, so the NYC-minus-WEST spread widens by 110 $/MWh on each of the 14 days, far below the historical maximum of 289.7. The short-NYC retail obligation P5 takes the main loss, and the 30% extra load scales its exposure. P2 offsets about 13% of it because it is only 25 MW. WEST on-peak is 60% below the level the load shock implies, since upstate has surplus supply behind the constraint.   },

   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A pipeline constraint and cold weather squeeze gas deliverability into the N.Y.C. load pocket for 15 days. Henry Hub rises 60 percent and a $8/MMBtu local basis lifts the cost of gas used by the heat-rate call P4. Gas-fired units in Zone J set the marginal price, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh, while WEST prices follow gas more gently. The retail obligation P5 is short 140 MW in N.Y.C. and only hedged at WEST, so it takes the loss. That loss is the largest of any position in the shock sensitivities, at about $4.7k per $/MWh-day. P2 recovers only part of it because it is just 25 MW. The WEST gains on P1 and P4 from higher gas offset a small part of the loss. This is the congestion and zone-volume channel. The January 2025 cold event shows a similar N.Y.C. versus WEST day-ahead gap of about $100/MWh, so the $150 shock is a deliberate stretch. Estimate: P5 about -10.5M, P2 +1.7M, P1 and P4 gains about +0.7M, net about -8M. This is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, so the estimate is uncertain.

A month-long gas supply problem hits downstate delivery only. Henry Hub rises 40 percent and the spread to N.Y.C. widens by $60/MWh for all 30 days. Upstate WEST has surplus hydro, wind and imports, and demand is soft, so WEST on-peak falls a further 40 percent on top of the gas-implied move. This hurts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. spread widening hurts the retail obligation P5 over the whole month, and the 25 MW spread position P2 offsets only a small part. Load stays at normal, so the loss comes from a long, persistent congestion channel that combines WEST weakness with N.Y.C. strength. This differs from scenario 1 because it is smaller per day, lasts twice as long, and adds a system-channel loss. Estimate: P5 about -8.4M, P2 +1.4M, P1 about -0.4M net of the gas gain, P4 about -0.3M, net about -7.5M. I stated a more cautious $6.5M because the effects are not additive and the ref_onpeak_pct and gas combination is unusual. Confidence is low.

A 14-day gas curtailment coincides with cold weather. Daily peak load is 10 percent above a typical winter day, which is inside the historical maximum ratio of 1.196. Gas rises 70 percent at Henry Hub, with a $5/MMBtu local basis hurting P4. Gas-fired generation in N.Y.C. is constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $130/MWh. The retail obligation P5 scales with load, so higher load enlarges its loss: it is about 1.1 times larger than at normal load. This is the zone-volume channel. Higher load and gas lift WEST prices and so give P1 and P4 gains, and P2 gains from the wider spread. Together these offset about $1.5M. Estimate: P5 about -9.6M, P2 +1.4M, P1 and P4 gains about +1M, net about -7M. This is extrapolated from 5-day sensitivities, so the figure is uncertain and confidence is low.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long downstate gas deliverability problem keeps N.Y.C. gas-fired units on expensive fuel while WEST stays comparatively well supplied. Henry Hub rises 25 percent and the local basis adds $4/MMBtu to the gas cost seen by the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $90/MWh on all 30 days, which is the main driver: the retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and only hedged at WEST, so it loses on every day. P2 recovers only a fraction because it is 25 MW against 140 MW. WEST on-peak falls a further 20 percent on top of the gas-implied move because surplus upstate supply and imports meet soft demand. This lowers the long swap P1 and offsets its gas gain. This is a persistent congestion and zone-volume loss with a mild system-channel drag. Estimate: P5 about -9.5M, P2 +1.7M, P1 and P4 roughly flat net, total about -7.5M. This is scaled from the earlier engine results, so it is uncertain.

A short, severe gas shortage hits the N.Y.C. pocket for 10 days, as in a pipeline freeze-off. Henry Hub doubles, up 100 percent, and the local basis adds $10/MMBtu to P4's gas cost, which cuts that heat-rate call's payoff relative to the unshocked path. Constrained gas in Zone J pushes the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread out by $250/MWh, inside the historical maximum of 400.6. P5 takes the loss because it is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST. P2 recovers about 15 percent of it. WEST on-peak falls a further 15 percent on top of the gas-implied move because upstate supply is not constrained, which trims the gain on P1. Load stays normal, so the loss comes from the spread alone and is front-loaded into a short window. Estimate: P5 about -9.7M, P2 +1.6M, P1 and P4 net about +0.5M, total about -7.5M, stated conservatively. Confidence is low because I scaled the 5-day sensitivities.

A 22-day gas supply shortfall coincides with a mild cold spell. Daily peak load is 12 percent above a typical winter day, inside the historical maximum of 1.196. Henry Hub rises 35 percent and a $6/MMBtu local basis lifts the gas cost seen by P4. N.Y.C. gas-fired units are fuel-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh. The retail obligation P5 scales with load, so its loss grows by about 12 percent over a normal-load case. This is the zone-volume channel at lower spread intensity but with a long duration. WEST prices rise with load and gas, so P1 and P4 gain, and P2 gains from the wider spread. Estimate: P5 about -9.6M, P2 +1.4M, P1 and P4 gains about +1M, total about -7.2M. I stated 6M to allow for non-additivity. Confidence is low because this extrapolates from the 5-day sensitivities.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 25-day downstate gas deliverability problem leaves N.Y.C. gas-fired units on expensive fuel while WEST is well supplied. Henry Hub rises 30 percent and a $2/MMBtu local basis adds to the gas cost seen by the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh on all 25 days. This is the main driver, because the retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST. P2 offsets only part of the loss because it is 25 MW against 140 MW. WEST on-peak falls a further 25 percent below the gas-implied path on soft upstate demand and surplus supply. This cuts the gain on the long swap P1 and on P4. Load stays at a normal level. This is a long congestion and zone-volume loss with a moderate system-channel drag. Estimate: P5 about -9M, P2 +1.9M, P1 and P4 about 0 net, total about -7M. This is scaled from earlier engine results, so it is uncertain.

A 30-day gas market dislocation lets WEST power weaken sharply relative to gas while N.Y.C. stays constrained. Henry Hub rises 15 percent and a $3/MMBtu local basis lifts the gas cost seen by P4. WEST on-peak falls a further 50 percent on top of the gas-implied move, because upstate supply is in surplus. This hurts the long swap P1 and cuts the P4 payoff against the unshocked path. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh on all 30 days, which hurts the retail obligation P5 on every day. P2 recovers only a small part of that loss. Load stays at a normal level. The system channel and the zone-volume channel therefore lose together, and no position gains from higher WEST prices. Estimate: P5 about -7.4M, P2 +1.6M, P1 about -1.5M, P4 about -0.6M, total about -7.5M, stated cautiously. Confidence is low because the effects are not additive.

A 12-day pipeline freeze-off cuts gas deliverability into the N.Y.C. pocket. Henry Hub rises 50 percent and a $6/MMBtu local basis lifts the gas cost seen by P4. Constrained gas in Zone J widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $200/MWh, inside the historical maximum of 400.6. Daily peak load is 3 percent above a typical winter day, which slightly enlarges the loss on the load-scaled P5. Real-time clears 30 percent above day-ahead on these days as supply is lost, which costs the day-ahead seller P3. WEST on-peak falls a further 10 percent below the gas-implied path, because upstate supply is unconstrained, and this trims the P1 gain. P5 is the main loss, and P2 recovers about 20 percent of it. Estimate: P5 about -9.6M, P2 +1.8M, P1 and P4 about +0.3M, total about -7.5M, stated cautiously at 6.5M. Confidence is low because the figure is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long gas supply problem tightens fuel into N.Y.C. while WEST power softens. Henry Hub rises 10 percent and a $1/MMBtu local basis slightly raises the gas cost seen by the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $65/MWh on all 30 days. This is the main driver, because the retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST. P2 recovers about a fifth of that loss. WEST on-peak falls a further 40 percent below the gas-implied path on surplus upstate supply and weak demand, which turns P1 and P4 from small gainers into losers. Load stays at a normal level. This is a mild-gas, long-duration case in which the zone-volume and system channels lose together. Estimate: P5 about -6.9M, P2 +1.2M, P1 about -1.1M, P4 about -0.45M, total about -7.2M. I stated $6.5M because the effects are not additive.

A 20-day local gas constraint hits only the N.Y.C. pocket, and Henry Hub does not move, so gas_hh_pct is zero. A $15/MMBtu local basis raises the gas cost seen by the heat-rate call P4 and cuts its payoff against the unshocked path. Constrained gas in Zone J widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $120/MWh on all 20 days, inside the historical maximum of 400.6. The retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST, so it takes most of the loss. P2 recovers about 15 percent. WEST on-peak falls a further 30 percent on ample upstate supply, which hurts the long swap P1 and P4. Load stays at a normal level. This is a basis-driven congestion and zone-volume loss with a system drag. Estimate: P5 about -8.8M, P2 +1.4M, P1 about -0.9M, P4 about -0.5M, total about -8.8M, stated conservatively at $7M. Confidence is low because this is extrapolated from the sensitivities.

A 14-day gas curtailment squeezes N.Y.C. generators hard. Henry Hub rises 45 percent and a $7/MMBtu local basis lifts the gas cost seen by P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $160/MWh on all 14 days, inside the historical maximum of 400.6. This drives the loss, because the retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST. P2 recovers about 15 percent. WEST on-peak falls a further 20 percent below the gas-implied path because upstate supply is not constrained, which limits the gains on P1 and P4. Load stays at a normal level and real-time stays at day-ahead, so the loss comes from the spread alone. This is a shorter and sharper congestion case than the longer scenarios above. Estimate: P5 about -8.5M, P2 +1.3M, P1 and P4 net about +0.3M, total about -6.9M, stated cautiously at $6M. Confidence is low because the figure is extrapolated.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads expected upstate (data centres, crypto, industrial) arrive about 900 MW slower than the Gold Book assumed (large_load_shock_mw = -900), and the peak load ratio is 0.95. Upstate WEST is left long supply, so WEST on-peak falls a further 20% (ref_onpeak_pct = -20) and the P1 swap and P4 call lose value. N.Y.C. is bound by local reliability and import limits and does not fall with WEST, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $60/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd = 60) for the full 30 days. This is the main loss. P5 is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price with only a WEST hedge, and the P2 gain covers only a fraction of that. Gas and DA/RT are left unshocked (0) because raising them would only lift the long WEST positions. No spikes are assumed. The loss is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities (about $3.4k per $/MWh-day of net spread loss, plus P1 and P4 on the WEST decline), so it is approximate.

scenario.narrative: Near-term large-load arrivals fall about 500 MW short (large_load_shock_mw = -500), with a peak load ratio of 0.98, so there is little load relief. WEST on-peak softens a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct = -15) as expected upstate demand does not materialise, which trims P1 and P4. Over a 12-day hot spell N.Y.C. stays tight because of local generation limits and transmission into the pocket, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $180/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd = 180), inside the summer historical maximum for the spread. The widening hits P5, the short fixed-price N.Y.C. load obligation, and exceeds the P2 gain by roughly $3.4k per $/MWh-day. Gas, DA/RT and spike shocks are zero, since price spikes would help the long WEST swap. The loss estimate is a linear extrapolation and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A large 2035-style load shortfall of about 1,400 MW (large_load_shock_mw = -1400) cuts the peak load ratio to 0.93. Weak demand and a softer gas market (gas_hh_pct = -30) push WEST on-peak down a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct = -35). The P1 swap and P4 heat-rate call lose on both the load and the gas channel. N.Y.C. is supported by local constraints, so the spread widens by $90/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd = 90) for 20 days. This is the main loss through P5, partly offset by P2 and by lower load scaling the P5 obligation. DA/RT is neutral (0) and no spikes occur, since spikes would help the long WEST positions. The stated loss adds the P1 and P4 declines to the spread loss using linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities. Interaction effects are not additive, so the estimate is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

A gas basis of +$2/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd = 2) is applied to P4 only, trimming its heat-rate payoff and adding a small loss on the gas channel. WEST on-peak, gas, DA/RT and spikes are left unshocked, since raising prices lifts the long WEST positions. The loss is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities, so it is approximate.

scenario.narrative: A 900 MW shortfall in large-load arrivals (large_load_shock_mw = -900, the 2030 shortfall range) leaves the peak load ratio at 1.0. For 15 days a heat-driven N.Y.C. constraint, with limited import capability into the pocket, widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $130/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd = 130), below the summer historical maximum. P5, the short fixed-price N.Y.C. load hedged only at WEST, takes the main loss, and P2 offsets about a fifth of it. WEST on-peak softens a further 8% (ref_onpeak_pct = -8) on the missing upstate demand, which trims P1 and P4. Gas, DA/RT and spikes are zero. The loss is a linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A 2035-style shortfall of about 1,200 MW in large-load arrivals (large_load_shock_mw = -1200) trims the peak load ratio to 0.97. Weak demand drives Henry Hub down 25% (gas_hh_pct = -25), WEST on-peak down a further 30% (ref_onpeak_pct = -30) and real-time 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct = -30). The long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 lose on all of these channels, and P3 gains a little. A gas basis of +$1.5/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd = 1.5) hits P4 only. N.Y.C. stays supported by local constraints, so the spread widens by $50/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd = 50) for 30 days, which hurts the short N.Y.C. load P5 and is partly offset by P2. The loss is split between the long WEST positions and the zone-volume obligation. It is a linear extrapolation and is approximate.
